items.definition: A weather derivative is a financial contract whose payout depends on a weather variable rather than a traded commodity price, most commonly temperature but also rainfall, snowfall, or hurricane activity. These contracts are typically negotiated bilaterally between two counterparties rather than exchange-traded, and are used mainly by utilities and insurers to manage weather exposure.
items.core_idea: Weather derivatives let a company monetize or hedge exposure to weather outcomes by tying payoff directly to a measured weather variable instead of a commodity price.
key_points: Payoff is indexed to a weather measurement (temperature is the most common basis).
Can also be written on rainfall, snowfall, or hurricane-related data.
Usually bilaterally negotiated, not standardized exchange products.
Primary users are utilities and insurance companies.
relationships: Distinct from but conceptually adjacent to insurance contracts (see 'Weather Derivatives vs. Insurance').
Addresses a risk type (combined volume and price risk) that standard commodity hedges don't cover.
trading_implications: A utility could use a temperature-linked derivative to offset the revenue/cost impact of an unusually mild or extreme season, complementing commodity hedges.
common_misunderstandings: Weather derivatives are not the same as insurance, even though both pay out based on external events.

items.topic: Weather Risk: Combined Volume and Price Exposure
items.definition: Weather is unusual as a risk factor for energy companies because a single weather event can simultaneously move both the quantity of energy needed (volume risk) and its price (price risk), making it hard to hedge with a standard financial instrument that typically addresses only one dimension.
items.core_idea: An extreme weather event can drive up both consumption and price at the same time, compounding the financial impact in a way ordinary single-variable hedges can't fully offset.
key_points: An unusually cold winter increases heating demand, which draws down stored natural gas faster than normal (volume effect).
The same cold snap can push natural gas prices higher as utilities compete for the dwindling supply of stored gas (price effect).

Because volume and price move together and are both driven by the same weather cause, standard financial hedges (which typically fix a price or a quantity separately) struggle to fully cover the combined exposure.
relationships: Motivates the use of weather derivatives as a complementary hedge alongside commodity price hedges.
Connects to natural gas storage dynamics during winter demand spikes.
trading_implications: Risk managers at gas utilities need to consider combined volume-and-price scenarios (e.g., a cold winter) rather than hedging price and volume as independent risks.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming a price hedge alone (e.g., a futures contract for a fixed quantity) fully protects against a weather-driven demand spike, when the volume actually needed also changes.

items.definition: While weather derivatives resemble insurance in that both pay out based on the occurrence of an external event, the author distinguishes them by probability and severity: weather derivatives typically cover events that occur with relatively high probability and cause comparatively modest losses, whereas insurance typically covers rare, high-severity events.
items.core_idea: Weather derivatives target frequent, moderate-impact weather deviations, while insurance targets rare, catastrophic losses.
key_points: Insurance example given: protection against flood or hurricane damage — a very large loss that might occur only about once every 100 years.

Weather derivative example given: protection for an airline against lost business if rainfall runs 10 percent above average — a smaller loss, but one that might recur several times within a 10-year period.
The distinction is about the probability/severity profile of the covered event, not the payout mechanism itself.
relationships: Builds directly on the definition of weather derivatives.
Uses insurance as a contrasting reference point rather than treating the two as identical.
trading_implications: Firms choosing between weather derivatives and insurance should match the product to the frequency/severity profile of the risk being managed — derivatives for frequent moderate risk, insurance for rare catastrophic risk.
common_misunderstandings: Treating weather derivatives as functionally identical to insurance; the author explicitly notes they differ in the probability and severity of the events they cover.

items.definition: Force majeure ('greater force' in French) is a standard contract clause that releases both parties from liability when extraordinary, uncontrollable events — such as war or natural disaster — prevent one or both from fulfilling their contractual obligations.
items.core_idea: A force majeure clause protects contract counterparties from breach liability when performance is made impossible by events outside anyone's control.
key_points: Common in energy and other commercial contracts.
Covers events like wars and natural disasters.
Applies specifically to events outside the control of either contracting party.
relationships: Relevant contract-risk concept alongside weather-driven disruptions discussed in this section.
trading_implications: Traders and structurers should check whether a physical delivery or supply contract includes a force majeure clause, since it determines liability if extreme weather or disaster prevents performance.
